summary: Extends remote-loop-free-alternate IP fast reroute with procedures to tell whether a PQ-node gives node protection, not just link protection.

eli5.summary: A backup route that still works if a whole intersection closes, not just one road.

questions: what is remote lfa node protection
how does remote lfa protect against node failure
default limit of pq nodes in remote lfa
subtitle: How a router can tell whether its remote backup route survives the loss of a whole neighbouring router, not just one link.

tldr.problem: Remote-LFA backup routes only guarantee link protection. If the whole next-hop router fails, the chosen PQ-node may send traffic down a path that also goes through the failed router, and nothing tells the computing router which case it is in.
tldr.mechanism: The computing router checks two path segments with distance inequalities: from itself to the PQ-node, and from the PQ-node to the destination. It runs one extra forward SPF per PQ-node, capped at a finite subset, and keeps only PQ-nodes whose paths avoid the primary next-hop node.
tldr.outcome: Routers can pick node-protecting remote-LFA paths and see the full path characteristics, so operator policy can choose among alternates more accurately.

facts.label: Extra computation
facts.value: One forward SPF per selected PQ-node

today: RFC 8102 is a Proposed Standard published in March 2017, and the unit metadata shows no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It extends the remote-LFA mechanism in RFC 7490.

sections.title: Why Link Protection Is Not Enough
sections.content:
Remote-LFA, defined in RFC 7490, gives a router a backup next hop (a PQ-node) when no ordinary loop-free alternate from RFC 5286 exists. The backup it finds guarantees only link protection. A PQ-node may not protect every destination if the whole primary next-hop node fails, and the base specification gives no way to tell.

The document also addresses a second gap. The manageability framework in RFC 7916 expects a router to collect the full path characteristics of every alternate and run an operator-configured selection policy. Today the forward SPF only reveals attributes such as SRLG and Admin-groups up to the PQ-node. Nothing is known about the segment from the PQ-node to the destination.

This RFC therefore describes a procedure to decide node protection for a given PQ-node and destination, and reuses the same procedure to gather complete path attributes.
sections.eli5: A spare route that avoids one broken street may still run through the same broken crossroads. The router needs a way to check, and to learn the whole spare route, not just the first half.

sections.title: The Node Protection Problem
sections.content:
The RFC starts from the topology of Figure 1, where router S protects the S-E link and R2 is the only PQ-node. R2 gives link protection for every destination reachable through E. But for destinations E and D1, the path from R2 goes through E itself, so if node E fails the backup fails too. The rule that follows is that the shortest path from the PQ-node to the destination MUST NOT traverse the primary next hop.

A second topology (Figure 2) adds a link between N and E. Now R3 is also a PQ-node, but the path from S to R3 can go through E, so one of the parallel equal-cost paths dies with E. The second rule is that the shortest paths from S to the chosen PQ-node MUST NOT traverse the primary next-hop node.

The RFC notes that node protection matters most where operators avoid non-stop routing because of its state synchronization and performance overhead.
sections.eli5: If the spare route still goes through the crossroads that closed, it is no spare at all. Both halves of the trip must stay away from the broken spot.

sections.title: P-Space, Q-Space and Their Node-Protecting Variants
sections.content:
The RFC extends the vocabulary of RFC 7490. The link-protecting extended P-space and the Q-space are the existing sets. A node is in the link-protecting PQ-space if it is in both.

For node protection it adds the node-protecting extended P-space: routers reachable from a direct neighbour of S (other than E) without traversing node E. Intersecting that with the Q-space gives the candidate node-protecting PQ-space. Being a candidate only guarantees that the segment from S to the PQ-node survives E failing. It says nothing yet about the segment from the PQ-node to the destination.

Each definition has a cost-based form. The node-protecting extended P-space test is D_opt(Ni,Y) < D_opt(Ni,E) + D_opt(E,Y), where D_opt is the distance on the optimal path, Ni is a neighbour of S other than E, and Y is the node being evaluated.
sections.eli5: The router draws a map of places it can reach without passing the broken crossroads, and places that can reach the crossroads without using the broken street. Good meeting points must be on both maps.

sections.title: Computing a Node-Protecting Path
sections.content:
An R-LFA path has two segments: the computing router to the PQ-node, and the PQ-node to the destination. Both must avoid the failed node.

Step 1, candidate PQ-nodes. The router applies the P-space inequality for every direct neighbour other than E, using metrics already gathered from the forward SPFs done for standard LFA. In Figure 2, R2 qualifies and R3 does not. Alternatively, an SPF that records the nodes on each shortest path lets the router simply check that E is absent.

Step 2, PQ-node to destination. The router MUST run a forward SPF on each candidate PQ-node and SHOULD then evaluate D_opt(Y,D) < D_opt(Y,E) + Distance_opt(E,D) for each destination. In the example, R2 gives node protection for R3 and D2 but not for E and D1. The procedure only filters existing remote-LFA alternates. It does not find new ones.

Several primary next hops. When a destination has several equal-cost next-hop nodes, a PQ-node MUST satisfy the inequality for all of them, and one that fails for any MUST NOT be chosen. The RFC's Figure 7 example shows R2 protecting D2 but not D1.
sections.eli5: The router checks the first half of the spare trip, then the second half. Only a spare route where both halves dodge every broken spot counts as safe.

sections.title: Limiting Computation Overhead
sections.content:
Running one forward SPF per PQ-node can be expensive, because a network usually has far more PQ-nodes than the computing router has direct neighbours. So implementations MUST pick a subset of PQ-nodes with a finite limit, MUST choose a default for that limit, and may let the user override it. The RFC suggests 16 as the default.

It also requires default preference criteria, though their exact form is left to the implementation. As a suggestion, implementations SHOULD score PQ-nodes by how many primary interfaces they cover (more is preferred), then by distance from the computing router (closer is preferred), then by the smaller router-id or IS-IS system-id. Implementations MAY allow a policy to override the criteria.
sections.eli5: Checking every possible meeting point would take too long, so the router checks only a short list of the most useful ones.

sections.title: Manageability of Alternate Paths
sections.content:
With plain remote-LFA, a router may have several usable PQ-nodes, and RFC 7916 lets an operator configure a policy to choose among them. That policy needs path characteristics for both segments. The first can be read from the regular forward SPF. The second, from the PQ-node to the destination, cannot be known without the extra SPF. Two alternates could look equal on the first segment while differing on the second.

The extra forward SPF from Section 2.3.2 therefore also collects links, nodes and path characteristics along the second segment. Because only a subset of PQ-nodes is examined, a very restrictive policy may leave a few destinations unprotected, which the RFC accepts as a trade-off between coverage and computational cost. The mechanism does not modify or invalidate RFC 7916.
sections.eli5: To choose the best spare route, the router needs to know what the whole route looks like, including the part after the meeting point.

sections.title: Security and IANA
sections.content: The RFC asks IANA to do nothing. Its security section is short: it introduces no change to any protocol specification and simply proposes an extra SPF rooted on each PQ-node discovered in the network.
sections.eli5: Nothing new is sent over the network. The router just does a bit more thinking on its own.

data.title: Distance conditions
data.code:
Node-protecting extended P-space (Y, via neighbour Ni):
  D_opt(Ni,Y) < D_opt(Ni,E) + D_opt(E,Y)

Q-space (Y):
  D_opt(Y,E) < D_opt(S,E) + D_opt(Y,S)

PQ-node Y to destination D:
  D_opt(Y,D) < D_opt(Y,E) + Distance_opt(E,D)
